background_notes.fact: If E:(0,∞)→ℝ is differentiable at every positive r with derivative zero, then f:ℝ→ℝ defined by f(r)=E(r) for r>0 and f(r)=0 for r≤0 has derivative zero and is continuous at every positive r. Consequently f is continuous on [a,b] and has derivative zero throughout (a,b) whenever 0<a<b.

background_notes.justification: For each r>0 the interval (r−r/2,r+r/2) lies in (0,∞), so f and E have identical difference quotients near r and hence the same derivative. A finite derivative implies continuity: f(r+h)−f(r)=h[(f(r+h)−f(r))/h] tends to zero because the bracket has a finite limit. Pointwise continuity at all points of [a,b] implies continuity restricted to that interval. No regularity at zero is asserted or required.
